task: Write one sentence of your own using the word placid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know placid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The night nurses trade shifts to care for the placid Otero baby, who naps through blood draws and gurgles at the thermometer.
Easygoing is milder than placid—an easygoing roommate shrugs at noise and mess but can still be rattled by real trouble, while a placid person's calm runs deeper and takes far more to shake.
Imperturbable goes further than easygoing—an imperturbable surgeon cannot be shaken by anything the day brings, while a placid person simply rests calm until something truly extraordinary intrudes.

Unflappable means impossible to fluster even when a crisis is in full swing—it is calm proven under pressure. Placid is quieter: a resting calm that was never disturbed in the first place. Unflappable describes performance in emergencies; placid describes an everyday temperament that nothing much tests.

Even-tempered means your moods stay level—no sharp highs or lows from day to day. Placid goes further: not merely level but genuinely undisturbed, a stillness that is simply the person's resting state. An even-tempered manager can still feel the stress; a placid one barely registers it.

Every Tuesday, a golden retriever named Waffle lies on a mat in the children's section while beginning readers take turns reading aloud to him.
The librarians chose Waffle for the job because he is placid to a degree his trainers called rare.
Toddlers have tugged his ears, a book cart once tipped over beside him, and the fire alarm has gone off twice.
Through all of it Waffle only sighs, rearranges his chin on his paws, and waits for the next page.
Children who stumble over words relax around a listener that nothing seems to disturb, and teachers say the shakiest readers volunteer most eagerly on Waffle days.
